title: What's new in pg_clickhouse v0.10.0: Subqueries, TPC-H Speedups, C Driver, and Aggregates
excerpt: Discover what's new in pg_clickhouse v0.10.0: 16 of 22 TPC-H queries now push down in full, plus a rebuilt C driver and broader aggregate support.
content_html:
Continuing our investment in pg_clickhouse, improving pushdown coverage for analytic workloads has remained our top focus, with full pushdown across the TPC-H benchmark suite as our immediate metric. We've had a lot of progress since our last update in June, including on the TPC-H scoreboard, which we haven't really talked about since our introductory post back in December, so that's where we'll start. With the release of v0.10.0, our scoreboard has moved from 12 of 22 TPC-H queries fully pushed down to 16, leaving only 6 to go to finish off the set.

Along the way, we also

  • rebuilt the binary driver on a new plain-C client library,
  • more than doubled the surface area of functions and aggregates that push down,
  • hardened the binary driver against a couple of concurrency bugs, detailed below.

Three more TPC-H queries now fully push down. All three were exceedingly inefficient before because, due to the shape of the query, pg_clickhouse had to fetch every row from ClickHouse individually and then evaluate the subquery on it locally (full chart):

QueryPostgreSQLpg_clickhouse 0.3pg_clickhouse 0.10Pushdown
Q2588 ms3,446 ms24 ms✔
Q172107 ms32,709 ms37 ms✔
Q22270 ms1,415 ms45 ms✼

( ✔ = whole query is a single foreign scan )
( ✼ = pushed down, but as more than one remote query; typically an outer scan plus one InitPlan scan.)

Q17 is the trophy: a correlated subquery averaging l_quantity per part that, back when it evaluated once per outer row against 6M line items at scale factor 1, took 32.7 seconds. Fully pushed down, it's 37 milliseconds. That's three orders of magnitude difference, and shows off a clear case where pg_clickhouse outperforms native PostgreSQL's own plan for the same query (2.1s).

Six queries remain unpushed: Q13, Q15, Q16, Q18, Q20, Q21. Q16 and Q18 show us the way forward; pg_clickhouse already pushes down the SQL shape they need (IN and NOT IN deparsed as anti/semi-joins, as in Q2 and Q17); what blocks them is that PostgreSQL flattens their subqueries into anti/semi-joins whose inputs are themselves joins, and the deparser doesn't yet walk a join tree on both sides of a join. Q15 and Q20 hit variants of the same issue. That's the next cohesive piece of subquery pushdown.

December's headline feature was teaching the planner to push a whole correlated EXISTS subquery down as a single LEFT SEMI JOIN instead of a nested loop with one ClickHouse round trip per outer row. This moved the needle from 3 of 22 TPC-H queries all the way to 12. The ten remaining queries shared one problem: the planner couldn't fold subqueries into a join at all, so it left a SubPlan behind. This is a piece of a query plan that describes a complete plan for a separate query that runs as part of executing the full query, usually once per row. Pushing that down was the fifth item on our roadmap, and we knocked it out (#289) as of this latest release (0.10.0). Now, subqueries in Postgres become subqueries in ClickHouse:

EXPLAIN (VERBOSE, COSTS OFF)
SELECT s.sale_id, s.amount FROM sales s
WHERE s.amount > (SELECT 1.5 * avg(s2.amount) FROM sales s2
                  WHERE s2.item_id = s.item_id)
ORDER BY s.sale_id;
Foreign Scan on subplan_test.sales s
   Output: s.sale_id, s.amount
   Remote SQL: SELECT sale_id, amount FROM subplan_test.sales r1 WHERE ((r1.amount > (SELECT (1.5 * avg(q1_1.amount)) FROM subplan_test.sales q1_1 WHERE ((q1_1.item_id = (r1.item_id)))))) ORDER BY r1.sale_id ASC NULLS LAST
   SubPlan expr_1
     ->  Foreign Scan
           Output: ((1.5 * avg(s2.amount)))
           Relations: Aggregate on (sales s2)
           Remote SQL: SELECT (1.5 * avg(amount)) FROM subplan_test.sales WHERE ((item_id = {p1:Int32}))
(8 rows)

The EXPLAIN still shows the SubPlan node (that's just PostgreSQL's bookkeeping for the correlation), but you can see the top Remote SQL contains the whole comparison, including the subquery, in one statement we ship to ClickHouse. The same mechanism enables pg_clickhouse to push down the whole of TPC-H Q2: one Foreign Scan and one remote query. NOT IN gets the same treatment via a LEFT ANTI JOIN (the negated cousin of v0.1.0's semi-join) whenever the planner can prove the transformation safe.

Note that none of this works below ClickHouse 25.8, which doesn't support the correlated-subquery SQL shape; pg_clickhouse checks the server version at plan time and falls back to local evaluation on older servers, the same as it always does for unsupported shapes.

Pushing down the SQL was the easy part. The harder part was making sure it computed the same answer PostgreSQL would (#315, #317), and that was its own rabbit hole. ClickHouse's IN operates on two-valued logic, PostgreSQL's on three-valued. That means x NOT IN (1, NULL) can be FALSE (x=1) or NULL in PostgreSQL, but never TRUE. Pushed down naively, these expressions can silently invert results wherever a NULL is involved in a comparison, WHERE NOT IN returning rows PostgreSQL would filter out, GROUP BY merging a NULL group into FALSE, etc. None of it shows up in ordinary testing, which is exactly why it's dangerous in a pushdown extension; the plan looks right and the output is subtly wrong.

V0.10's fix tracks how each expression's result gets consumed, so we know how much hedging the query has to do to keep results consistent. This is where the rabbit hole took on a menger sponge vibe:

  • A filter condition can treat NULL like FALSE for free, so ClickHouse behavior is fine in conditions outside of NOT.
  • A value position or a negation needs extra checking for null values to inject the correct Postgres value into the result.
  • If pg_clickhouse can prove the operands can't be NULL (by tracing them to a non-NULL constant, or a column with a NOT NULL constraint that no outer join has re-nulled, or a non-nullable operation over these...), it can skip adding the guards that inject the Postgres behavior.

So a query with our guards and Postgres behavior implemented looks like this:

EXPLAIN (VERBOSE, COSTS OFF)
SELECT id FROM tnull WHERE xn NOT IN (1, NULL) ORDER BY id;
Foreign Scan on in_null_test.tnull
   Output: id
   Remote SQL: SELECT id FROM in_null_test.tnull WHERE ((CASE WHEN xn IS NULL AND notEmpty([1,NULL]) THEN NULL WHEN countEqual([1,NULL], xn) > 0 THEN false WHEN countEqual([1,NULL], NULL) > 0 THEN NULL ELSE true END)) ORDER BY id ASC NULLS LAST
(3 rows)

While a common, NULL-free case can ship as a plain native IN:

EXPLAIN (VERBOSE, COSTS OFF)
SELECT id FROM tnull WHERE xn NOT IN (1, 500) ORDER BY id;
Foreign Scan on in_null_test.tnull
   Output: id
   Remote SQL: SELECT id FROM in_null_test.tnull WHERE ((xn NOT IN (1,500))) ORDER BY id ASC NULLS LAST
(3 rows)

A follow-up (#317) generalized this behavior to the whole IN family of operators (IN, NOT IN, = ANY, = ALL, <> ANY, <> ALL), scalar and array forms alike, allowing them to push down unconditionally instead of falling back to local evaluation when non-nullability couldn't be proven.

Additionally, we had a little bug where <> ANY(array) actually computed <> ALL, which we knocked out while we were in the area.

All of this rests on the assumption that ClickHouse's IN actually behaves the two-valued way we've been describing. A server-level setting (transform_null_in) can change that. So we added transform_null_in 0 to the default pg_clickhouse.session_settings, to make sure a ClickHouse server profile can't silently pull the rug out from under the guards we just described.

Alongside the join and subquery work, the list of individual functions, operators, and aggregates that push down grew substantially. Too substantially to list in full here (see the CHANGELOG for detail), but here's a sample of where the breadth came from:

  • Regex: We've covered a lot of updates here in our earlier newspost, so give that a look!

  • Aggregates:

    • Statistical aggregates (#290)
      • corr, covar_pop/samp
      • stddev_pop/samp
      • var_pop/samp
      • any_value
    • Ordered-set aggregates (#291): Mapped to ClickHouse's parametric forms.
      • percentile_cont/disc → quantile(s)/quantileExactLow

  • Partitionwise aggregation (#298): Useful if you've moved analytics-heavy partitions to ClickHouse and kept transaction-heavy partitions in Postgres.

    • Foreign partition compute: A query aggregating over a partitioned table with a mix of local and foreign partitions now computes the foreign partition's share on ClickHouse instead of fetching its rows.
      • This is for decomposable aggregates like count, sum, min, max, avg over integers.
      • Requires enable_partitionwise_aggregate.

  • Everything else:

    • Formatting and encoding: encode(bytea, 'hex'|'base64'|'base64url') (#302).
    • Strings: Three-argument ltrim/rtrim/btrim (#307),
    • Cost estimation: Fixed some cost functions to keep the planner picking cheaper option for MIN/MAX on ClickHouse. (#310)
    • Dates and times:
      • Interval arithmetic extended to date/timestamp operands and subtraction (#301)
      • Retuned the CURRENT_*/now()/clock_timestamp() family for session time zone and sub-second precision.

Beneath all of that lies an important architectural change: builtin function pushdown is now opt-in (#245). Early on, any Postgres builtin whose name matched a ClickHouse function shipped by default, which meant a signature or behavioral difference could silently change results. The concrete case that forced the change was trig functions (asin/acos/atanh/acosh): Postgres raises an error when these are called on a value outside their domain, while ClickHouse returns NaN. Since v0.3.0, a function only pushes down if it's explicitly mapped, which is slower to grow the list but means the list is trustworthy in terms of preserving Postgres semantics.

Our introductory post described modernizing on the old clickhouse_fdw lineage in part by adopting clickhouse-cpp for native-protocol access. That's already out of date: in v0.3.1, we replaced it wholesale with ClickHouse/clickhouse-c, a new C client vendored as a git submodule (#254). The switch wasn't just a dependency bump; mixing C++ exception handling with PostgreSQL's own setjmp/longjmp-based error handling had been a source of crashes, and clickhouse-cpp's monolithic result buffering meant memory use scaled with result size. By contrast, clickhouse-c streams results block by block instead, and dropped the vendored library's build time and size by over 75%.

We continued that consolidation after the initial clickhouse-c switch: the HTTP driver now speaks ClickHouse's Native format, too: the same encoding and decoding the binary driver already used, in place of the old TSV-based path (#328). One casualty of that change is fetch_size, the batching option from the HTTP driver's earlier streaming work. The native decoder streams one curl chunk at a time regardless, so there's nothing left for that setting to configure, and it's now deprecated. On the write side, the binary driver now flushes buffered INSERT/COPY FROM data past 64MiB (#303), instead of holding an entire batch in memory. Both drivers gained explicit compression (none/lz4/zstd) (#268) and TLS controls (secure = on/off/auto, min_tls_version) (#272), replacing a heuristic that inferred TLS from the hostname and port. Type coverage widened as well: we now support multidimensional arrays for both reads and writes in both drivers (#233), and Array(Nullable(T)) inserts over the binary protocol (#316).

Both drivers now sharing one binary encoding path is also what made several reliability fixes possible this cycle. Concurrent foreign scans on the binary driver (e.g. a correlated subquery or a nested-loop join over two foreign tables) used to collide on a single shared connection and crash; each concurrent scan now gets its own connection (#296), which also closed a related use-after-free in a rescanned foreign scan's batch memory context. We also have a fix for a particular query structure failing during execution due to choosing an invalid relation OID when choosing a user to run the query as (#319).

Getting more into the nitty-gritty, we also closed a subsecond-precision loss when inserting timestamps over HTTP (#300), and to top it all off, a broader static-analysis pass over the codebase turned up and fixed a handful of other latent bugs (#313); these hadn't showed up in the field, but were worth closing before they could.

A handful of additions expand what you can do, not just what pushes down automatically: clickhouse_query(server, sql) runs an arbitrary query against a configured server and types the result by your column definition list, now with binary-driver support (#309). That column definition list is unavoidable (Postgres needs to know the shape of the rows before it can start fetching them), but it also means clickhouse_query() has no way to run something like CREATE TABLE, which returns no rows and has no shape to declare. That's what its new companion, clickhouse_perform(server, sql), is for: a procedure, called with CALL instead of SELECT, for statements you run for effect rather than for rows (#329). Additionally, largely for internal use in conditional logic, clickhouse_server_version(server) reports the connected server's version (#293).

If you've been using clickhouse_raw_query() for this, it's now deprecated and will be removed next release (#329). Move to clickhouse_query() or CALL clickhouse_perform() instead; both go through a configured foreign server, with its own connection handling and driver selection, rather than a raw, ad-hoc connection string.

We've posted elsewhere about a number of these features from past releases, but forgot to mention them here, and wanted to set the record straight.

  • JSON:

    • Operators and functions: ->/->> and jsonb_extract_path[_text]() map onto ClickHouse's sub-column syntax (#169, #176).
    • Types: ClickHouse's native JSON type maps onto Postgres json with the same operator support.

  • Arrays:

    • New functions and operators: Over a dozen functions push down:
      • array_cat
      • append
      • remove
      • to_string
      • length
      • hasAll/hasAny for @>/<@/&&
      • Slice syntax (arr[L:U]) as arraySlice()
      • Still more...

  • Aggregates:

    • Window functions (#175): The full set pushes down, including these and their friends:
      • ROW_NUMBER
      • RANK
      • LEAD/LAG
      • NTILE
    • Booleans and String (#184): bool_and, bool_or, string_agg

  • Everything else:

    • to_char() with format-string validation (#244)
    • split_part() (#206)
    • fuzzystrmatch's soundex()/levenshtein() (#210).

Beyond the six remaining TPC-H queries, much of the original roadmap remains open: the remaining uncovered PostgreSQL functions, lightweight DELETE/UPDATE, and UNION pushdown. The join-tree-on-both-sides limitation blocking Q15/16/18/20 is the most consequential piece and the natural next post in this series, if we don't knock out all six by next release.

blocks.html_en: December's headline feature was teaching the planner to push a whole correlated EXISTS subquery down as a single LEFT SEMI JOIN instead of a nested loop with one ClickHouse round trip per outer row. This moved the needle from 3 of 22 TPC-H queries all the way to 12. The ten remaining queries shared one problem: the planner couldn't fold subqueries into a join at all, so it left a SubPlan behind. This is a piece of a query plan that describes a complete plan for a separate query that runs as part of executing the full query, usually once per row. blocks.html_en: Pushing down the SQL was the easy part. The harder part was making sure it computed the same answer PostgreSQL would (#315, #317), and that was its own rabbit hole. ClickHouse's IN operates on two-valued logic, PostgreSQL's on three-valued. That means x NOT IN (1, NULL) can be FALSE (x=1) or NULL in PostgreSQL, but never TRUE. Pushed down naively, these expressions can silently invert results wherever a NULL is involved in a comparison, WHERE NOT IN returning rows PostgreSQL would filter out, GROUP BY merging a NULL group into FALSE, etc. None of it shows up in ordinary testing, which is exactly why it's dangerous in a pushdown extension; the plan looks right and the output is subtly wrong.

blocks.html_en: Beneath all of that lies an important architectural change: builtin function pushdown is now opt-in (#245). Early on, any Postgres builtin whose name matched a ClickHouse function shipped by default, which meant a signature or behavioral difference could silently change results. The concrete case that forced the change was trig functions (asin/acos/atanh/acosh): Postgres raises an error when these are called on a value outside their domain, while ClickHouse returns NaN. Since v0.3.0, a function only pushes down if it's explicitly mapped, which is slower to grow the list but means the list is trustworthy in terms of preserving Postgres semantics.

blocks.html_en: Our introductory post described modernizing on the old clickhouse_fdw lineage in part by adopting clickhouse-cpp for native-protocol access. That's already out of date: in v0.3.1, we replaced it wholesale with ClickHouse/clickhouse-c, a new C client vendored as a git submodule (#254). The switch wasn't just a dependency bump; mixing C++ exception handling with PostgreSQL's own setjmp/longjmp-based error handling had been a source of crashes, and clickhouse-cpp's monolithic result buffering meant memory use scaled with result size. By contrast, clickhouse-c streams results block by block instead, and dropped the vendored library's build time and size by over 75%.

blocks.html_en: We continued that consolidation after the initial clickhouse-c switch: the HTTP driver now speaks ClickHouse's Native format, too: the same encoding and decoding the binary driver already used, in place of the old TSV-based path (#328). One casualty of that change is fetch_size, the batching option from the HTTP driver's earlier streaming work. The native decoder streams one curl chunk at a time regardless, so there's nothing left for that setting to configure, and it's now deprecated. On the write side, the binary driver now flushes buffered INSERT/COPY FROM data past 64MiB (#303), instead of holding an entire batch in memory. Both drivers gained explicit compression (none/lz4/zstd) (#268) and TLS controls (secure = on/off/auto, min_tls_version) (#272), replacing a heuristic that inferred TLS from the hostname and port. Type coverage widened as well: we now support multidimensional arrays for both reads and writes in both drivers (#233), and Array(Nullable(T)) inserts over the binary protocol (#316).

blocks.html_en: Both drivers now sharing one binary encoding path is also what made several reliability fixes possible this cycle. Concurrent foreign scans on the binary driver (e.g. a correlated subquery or a nested-loop join over two foreign tables) used to collide on a single shared connection and crash; each concurrent scan now gets its own connection (#296), which also closed a related use-after-free in a rescanned foreign scan's batch memory context. We also have a fix for a particular query structure failing during execution due to choosing an invalid relation OID when choosing a user to run the query as (#319).

blocks.html_en: Getting more into the nitty-gritty, we also closed a subsecond-precision loss when inserting timestamps over HTTP (#300), and to top it all off, a broader static-analysis pass over the codebase turned up and fixed a handful of other latent bugs (#313); these hadn't showed up in the field, but were worth closing before they could.

blocks.html_en: A handful of additions expand what you can do, not just what pushes down automatically: clickhouse_query(server, sql) runs an arbitrary query against a configured server and types the result by your column definition list, now with binary-driver support (#309). That column definition list is unavoidable (Postgres needs to know the shape of the rows before it can start fetching them), but it also means clickhouse_query() has no way to run something like CREATE TABLE, which returns no rows and has no shape to declare. That's what its new companion, clickhouse_perform(server, sql), is for: a procedure, called with CALL instead of SELECT, for statements you run for effect rather than for rows (#329). Additionally, largely for internal use in conditional logic, clickhouse_server_version(server) reports the connected server's version (#293).

content_html_zh:
继续我们对 pg_clickhouse 的投资，提高分析工作负载的下推覆盖率仍然是我们的首要关注点，并将 TPC-H 基准套件的全面下推作为我们的直接指标。 自 6 月份的上次更新以来，我们已经取得了很多进展，包括 TPC-H 记分牌，自从 12 月份的介绍性帖子以来我们还没有真正讨论过这一点，所以这就是我们开始的地方。 随着 v0.10.0 的发布，我们的记分板已从 22 个 TPC-H 查询中的 12 个完全减少到 16 个，只剩下 6 个可以完成该组查询。

一路走来，我们也

  • 在新的纯 C 客户端库上重建二进制驱动程序，
  • 向下推动的功能和聚合体的表面积增加了一倍多，
  • 针对几个并发错误强化了二进制驱动程序，详细信息如下。

现在，另外三个 TPC-H 查询已完全下推。 这三个方法之前效率都非常低，因为由于查询的形状，pg_clickhouse 必须单独从 ClickHouse 获取每一行，然后在本地评估子查询（完整图表）：

QueryPostgreSQLpg_clickhouse 0.3pg_clickhouse 0.10下推
Q2588 ms3,446 ms24 ms✔
Q172107 ms32,709 ms37 ms✔
Q22270 ms1,415 ms45 ms✼

( ✔ = 整个查询是一次外部扫描) ( ✼ = 下推，但作为多个远程查询；通常是外部扫描加上一次 InitPlan 扫描。)

Q17 是奖杯：一个平均每个部分 l_quantity 的相关子查询，当它在比例因子 1 下针对 6M 个行项目对每个外部行进行一次评估时，花费了 32.7 秒。 完全按下去，是 37 毫秒。 这是三个数量级的差异，并且清楚地表明 pg_clickhouse 优于本机 PostgreSQL 自己的相同查询计划（2.1 秒）。

六个查询仍未推送：Q13、Q15、Q16、Q18、Q20、Q21。 Q16和Q18为我们指明了前进的方向； pg_clickhouse 已经下推了他们需要的 SQL 形状（IN 和 NOT IN 被解析为反/半连接，如 Q2 和 Q17）；阻碍它们的是 PostgreSQL 将它们的子查询扁平化为反/半连接，其输入本身就是连接，并且解析器尚未在连接两侧遍历连接树。 Q15 和 Q20 遇到了同一问题的变体。 这是子查询下推的下一个有凝聚力的部分。

12 月的头条新闻是教规划器将整个相关的 EXISTS 子查询向下推为单个 LEFT SEMI JOIN，而不是每个外行一次 ClickHouse 往返的嵌套循环。 这使得 22 个 TPC-H 查询中的 3 个一直增加到 12 个。 剩下的十个查询有一个共同的问题：规划器根本无法将子查询折叠到联接中，因此它留下了一个子计划。 这是查询计划的一部分，描述了作为执行完整查询的一部分运行的单独查询的完整计划，通常每行一次。 推动这一点是我们路线图上的第五项，我们在最新版本 (0.10.0) 中将其淘汰 (#289)。 现在，Postgres 中的子查询成为 ClickHouse 中的子查询：

EXPLAIN (VERBOSE, COSTS OFF)
SELECT s.sale_id, s.amount FROM sales s
WHERE s.amount > (SELECT 1.5 * avg(s2.amount) FROM sales s2
                  WHERE s2.item_id = s.item_id)
ORDER BY s.sale_id;
Foreign Scan on subplan_test.sales s
   Output: s.sale_id, s.amount
   Remote SQL: SELECT sale_id, amount FROM subplan_test.sales r1 WHERE ((r1.amount > (SELECT (1.5 * avg(q1_1.amount)) FROM subplan_test.sales q1_1 WHERE ((q1_1.item_id = (r1.item_id)))))) ORDER BY r1.sale_id ASC NULLS LAST
   SubPlan expr_1
     ->  Foreign Scan
           Output: ((1.5 * avg(s2.amount)))
           Relations: Aggregate on (sales s2)
           Remote SQL: SELECT (1.5 * avg(amount)) FROM subplan_test.sales WHERE ((item_id = {p1:Int32}))
(8 rows)

EXPLAIN 仍然显示 SubPlan 节点（这只是 PostgreSQL 的相关性簿记），但您可以看到顶部的 Remote SQL 在我们发送到 ClickHouse 的一条语句中包含整个比较，包括子查询。 同样的机制使得 pg_clickhouse 能够下推整个 TPC-H Q2：一次外部扫描和一次远程查询。 只要规划器可以证明转换安全，NOT IN 就会通过 LEFT ANTI JOIN（v0.1.0 半连接的否定表亲）获得相同的处理。

请注意，这些在 ClickHouse 25.8 以下都不起作用，因为它不支持相关子查询 SQL 形状； pg_clickhouse 在计划时检查服务器版本，并回退到旧服务器上的本地评估，就像它对不受支持的形状所做的那样。

下推 SQL 是最简单的部分。 更困难的部分是确保它计算出与 PostgreSQL 相同的答案（#315、#317），而这就是它自己的兔子洞。 ClickHouse 的 IN 运行在二值逻辑上，PostgreSQL 运行在三值逻辑上。 这意味着 x NOT IN (1, NULL) 在 PostgreSQL 中可以为 FALSE (x=1) 或 NULL，但绝不能为 TRUE。 天真地向下推，这些表达式可以在比较中涉及 NULL 的地方默默地反转结果，WHERE NOT IN 返回行 PostgreSQL 会过滤掉，GROUP BY 将 NULL 组合并到 FALSE 等。它们都不会出现在普通测试中，这正是它在下推扩展中危险的原因；计划看起来是正确的，但输出却有微妙的错误。

V0.10 的修复跟踪每个表达式的结果如何被消耗，因此我们知道查询必须进行多少对冲才能保持结果一致。 这就是兔子洞呈现出门格尔海绵氛围的地方：

  • 过滤条件可以像对待 FALSE 一样免费对待 NULL，因此 ClickHouse 行为在 NOT 之外的条件下没有问题。
  • 值位置或否定需要额外检查空值，以将正确的 Postgres 值注入到结果中。
  • 如果 pg_clickhouse 可以证明操作数不能为 NULL（通过将它们跟踪到非 NULL 常量，或者具有 NOT NULL 约束且没有外连接重新为空的列，或者对这些操作进行不可空操作...），它可以跳过添加注入 Postgres 行为的防护。

因此，使用我们的守卫和 Postgres 行为实现的查询如下所示：

EXPLAIN (VERBOSE, COSTS OFF)
SELECT id FROM tnull WHERE xn NOT IN (1, NULL) ORDER BY id;
Foreign Scan on in_null_test.tnull
   Output: id
   Remote SQL: SELECT id FROM in_null_test.tnull WHERE ((CASE WHEN xn IS NULL AND notEmpty([1,NULL]) THEN NULL WHEN countEqual([1,NULL], xn) > 0 THEN false WHEN countEqual([1,NULL], NULL) > 0 THEN NULL ELSE true END)) ORDER BY id ASC NULLS LAST
(3 rows)

虽然常见的、无 NULL 的情况可以作为普通的本机 IN 提供：

EXPLAIN (VERBOSE, COSTS OFF)
SELECT id FROM tnull WHERE xn NOT IN (1, 500) ORDER BY id;
Foreign Scan on in_null_test.tnull
   Output: id
   Remote SQL: SELECT id FROM in_null_test.tnull WHERE ((xn NOT IN (1,500))) ORDER BY id ASC NULLS LAST
(3 rows)

后续版本 (#317) 将这种行为推广到整个 IN 系列运算符（IN、NOT IN、= ANY、= ALL、<> ANY、<> ALL）、标量和数组形式，允许它们无条件下推，而不是在无法证明非空性时回退到局部求值。

此外，我们还有一个小错误，其中 <> ANY(array) 实际上计算 <> ALL，我们在该区域时将其消除。

所有这一切都基于这样的假设：ClickHouse 的 IN 实际上以我们所描述的二值方式运行。 服务器级设置 (transform_null_in) 可以改变这一点。 因此，我们将transform_null_in 0 添加到默认的pg_clickhouse.session_settings 中，以确保ClickHouse 服务器配置文件无法悄悄地从我们刚才描述的防护罩下拉出地毯。

除了连接和子查询工作之外，下推的各个函数、运算符和聚合的列表也大幅增长。 内容太多，无法在此处完整列出（有关详细信息，请参阅变更日志），但这里是广度来源的示例：

  • 正则表达式：我们在之前的新闻文章中介绍了很多更新，所以请看一下！
  • 聚合：统计聚合 (#290) corr、covar_pop/samp stddev_pop/samp var_pop/samp any_value 有序集聚合 (#291)：映射到 ClickHouse 的参数形式。 percentile_cont/disc → 分位数/quantileExactLow
  • 分区聚合 (#298)：如果您已将分析密集型分区移至 ClickHouse 并将事务密集型分区保留在 Postgres 中，则非常有用。 外部分区计算：在混合了本地和外部分区的分区表上聚合的查询现在计算 ClickHouse 上外部分区的份额，而不是获取其行。 这适用于可分解的聚合，例如整数上的计数、总和、最小值、最大值、平均值。 需要启用_partitionwise_aggregate。
  • 其他一切：格式化和编码：encode(bytea, 'hex'|'base64'|'base64url') (#302)。 字符串：三参数 ltrim/rtrim/btrim (#307)，成本估算：修复了一些成本函数，以使规划者在 ClickHouse 上为 MIN/MAX 选择更便宜的选项。 (#310) 日期和时间：间隔算术扩展到日期/时间戳操作数和减法 (#301) 重新调整了会话时区和亚秒精度的 CURRENT_*/now()/clock_timestamp() 系列。

所有这些的背后隐藏着一个重要的架构变化：内置函数下推现在是可选的（#245）。 早期，任何名称与默认提供的 ClickHouse 函数匹配的 Postgres 内置函数，这意味着签名或行为差异可能会悄悄地改变结果。 强制更改的具体情况是三角函数（asin/acos/atanh/acosh）：当在其域之外的值上调用这些函数时，Postgres 会引发错误，而 ClickHouse 返回 NaN。 从 v0.3.0 开始，函数仅在显式映射时才会下推，这会导致列表增长速度较慢，但​​意味着该列表在保留 Postgres 语义方面是值得信赖的。

我们的介绍性文章描述了通过采用 clickhouse-cpp 进行本机协议访问来对旧的 clickhouse_fdw 血统进行现代化改造。 这已经过时了：在 v0.3.1 中，我们用 ClickHouse/clickhouse-c 批量替换了它，这是一个作为 git 子模块出售的新 C 客户端 (#254)。 这种转变不仅仅是依赖的冲突；将 C++ 异常处理与 PostgreSQL 自己的基于 setjmp/longjmp 的错误处理混合在一起是崩溃的根源，而 clickhouse-cpp 的整体结果缓冲意味着内存使用量会随着结果大小而缩放。 相比之下，clickhouse-c 则逐块流式传输结果，并将供应库的构建时间和大小减少了 75% 以上。

在最初的 clickhouse-c 切换之后，我们继续进行整合：HTTP 驱动程序现在也使用 ClickHouse 的本机格式：与已使用的二进制驱动程序相同的编码和解码，代替旧的基于 TSV 的路径 (#328)。 这一变化的受害者之一是 fetch_size，它是 HTTP 驱动程序早期流工作中的批处理选项。 无论如何，本机解码器一次会流式传输一个curl 块，因此该设置无需配置，现在已弃用。 在写入方面，二进制驱动程序现在刷新缓冲的 INSERT/COPY FROM 数据超过 64MiB (#303)，而不是将整个批次保存在内存中。 两个驱动程序都获得了显式压缩（none/lz4/zstd）（#268）和 TLS 控制（secure = on/off/auto, min_tls_version）（#272），取代了从主机名和端口推断 TLS 的启发式方法。 类型覆盖范围也扩大了：我们现在支持在两个驱动程序中进行读取和写入的多维数组（#233），以及通过二进制协议插入数组（Nullable（T））（#316）。

两个驱动程序现在共享一个二进制编码路径，这也使得本周期中的多项可靠性修复成为可能。 二进制驱动程序上的并发外部扫描（例如，相关子查询或两个外部表上的嵌套循环连接）用于在单个共享连接上发生冲突并崩溃；现在，每个并发扫描都有自己的连接（#296），这也会在重新扫描的外部扫描的批处理内存上下文中关闭相关的释放后使用。 我们还修复了特定查询结构在执行过程中由于在选择用户运行查询时选择无效关系 OID 而失败的问题 (#319)。

更深入地了解细节，我们还解决了通过 HTTP 插入时间戳时的亚秒精度损失（#300），最重要的是，对代码库进行了更广泛的静态分析，并修复了一些其他潜在错误（#313）；这些尚未出现在现场，但值得在出现之前关闭。

一些添加扩展了您可以执行的操作，而不仅仅是自动下推的操作：clickhouse_query(server, sql) 针对已配置的服务器运行任意查询，并通过列定义列表键入结果，现在具有二进制驱动程序支持 (#309)。 该列定义列表是不可避免的（Postgres 在开始获取行之前需要知道行的形状），但这也意味着 clickhouse_query() 无法运行 CREATE TABLE 之类的东西，它不返回任何行，也没有要声明的形状。 这就是它的新伴侣 clickhouse_perform(server, sql) 的用途：使用 CALL 而不是 SELECT 调用的过程，用于为效果而不是行而运行的语句 (#329)。 此外，主要供条件逻辑内部使用，clickhouse_server_version(server) 报告连接的服务器的版本 (#293)。

如果您一直使用 clickhouse_raw_query() 来实现此目的，那么它现在已被弃用，并将在下一个版本中删除（#329）。 移至 clickhouse_query() 或调用 clickhouse_perform() ；两者都通过配置的外部服务器，具有自己的连接处理和驱动程序选择，而不是原始的临时连接字符串。

我们已经在其他地方发布了有关过去版本中的一些功能的信息，但忘记在这里提及它们，并希望澄清事实。

  • JSON：运算符和函数：->/->> 和 jsonb_extract_path[_text]() 映射到 ClickHouse 的子列语法（#169、#176）。 类型：ClickHouse 的原生 JSON 类型映射到具有相同运算符支持的 Postgres json。
  • 数组：新函数和运算符：十多个函数下推： array_cat 添加删除 to_string 长度 hasAll/hasAny for @>/<@/&& 切片语法 (arr[L:U]) as arraySlice() 还有更多...
  • 聚合：窗口函数 (#175)：全套下推，包括这些函数和它们的朋友：ROW_NUMBER RANK LEAD/LAG NTILE 布尔值和字符串 (#184)：bool_and、bool_or、string_agg
  • 其他一切：带有格式字符串验证的 to_char() (#244) split_part() (#206) fuzzystrmatch 的 soundex()/levenshtein() (#210)。

除了剩下的六个 TPC-H 查询之外，原始路线图的大部分仍然开放：其余未覆盖的 PostgreSQL 函数、轻量级 DELETE/UPDATE 和 UNION 下推。 如果我们不在下一个版本中淘汰所有六个，则阻止 Q15/16/18/20 的 join-tree-on-sides 限制是本系列中最重要的部分，也是本系列中自然的下一篇文章。
